Recipient and theme lengths are paired on each dative token. The **covariance** summarizes whether their deviations from their respective means tend to have the same sign.

## Definition

For random variables $R$ and $T$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}\left[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])\right].
$$

Expanding the product gives the equivalent identity

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(R,T)
=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
$$

More explicitly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[(R-\mathbb{E}[R])(T-\mathbb{E}[T])]
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]
-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&\quad-\mathbb{E}[T]\mathbb{E}[R]
+\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]\\
&=\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T].
\end{aligned}
$$

For constants $a,b,c,d$,

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(aR+b,cT+d)
=ac\,\operatorname{Cov}(R,T).
$$

Covariance has units equal to the product of the two measurement units. Here both lengths are measured in words, so covariance is measured in words squared.

## Empirical covariance of dative lengths

```{r}
#| label: dative-covariance
library(ggplot2)

dative <- read.csv(
  "data/english-dative/dative-alternation.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)
R <- dative$recipient_length_words
T <- dative$theme_length_words
mean_R <- mean(R)
mean_T <- mean(T)
covariance_population <- mean((R - mean_R) * (T - mean_T))
covariance_identity <- mean(R * T) - mean_R * mean_T

joint <- as.data.frame(table(recipient = R, theme = T), responseName = "count")
joint$recipient <- as.integer(as.character(joint$recipient))
joint$theme <- as.integer(as.character(joint$theme))
joint <- subset(joint, count > 0)

stopifnot(
  length(R) == 3263L,
  abs(covariance_population - covariance_identity) < 1e-12,
  abs(cov(R, T) * (length(R) - 1) / length(R) -
        covariance_population) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(mean_R, mean_T, covariance_population,
           sample_covariance = cov(R, T))
```

The empirical population covariance is `r sprintf("%.3f", covariance_population)` words squared. Its positive sign means that same-direction deviations make a slightly larger average contribution than opposite-direction deviations.

```{r}
#| label: plot-dative-covariance
#| fig-cap: "Observed dative length pairs. Point area shows token count; accent lines mark the two empirical means."
ggplot(joint, aes(theme, recipient, size = count)) +
  geom_point(color = "grey35", alpha = 0.65) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean_T, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_R, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.65) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 7) +
  labs(x = "Theme length (words)", y = "Recipient length (words)",
       size = "Token count") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The cloud extends far on both axes but has little diagonal organization. Covariance alone does not show nonlinear dependence, and its magnitude cannot be compared across variables with different units or scales.

## Sample covariance

When rows are treated as a sample for estimating a population covariance, the familiar estimator is

$$
s_{R,T}
=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(R_i-\overline R)(T_i-\overline T).
$$

The page reports the empirical population covariance of the pinned table because its immediate target is that table's joint distribution. Later inferential work must state a sampling unit and accommodate repeated verbs and speakers.

## Check your understanding

1. Verify covariance with the $\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]$ identity.
2. Identify which quadrants around the mean lines contribute positively.
3. Explain the difference between the two denominators used above.
4. Why can a covariance near zero coexist with dependence?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\mathbb{E}[RT]-\mathbb{E}[R]\mathbb{E}[T]=0.284045$ words squared, matching the mean centered product. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Observations above both means and observations below both means contribute positively because the two centered factors have the same sign. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Dividing by $n$ treats the represented rows as the empirical population, whereas dividing by $n-1$ applies the usual sample-covariance degrees-of-freedom correction. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Covariance can be near zero under strong nonlinear or sign-canceling dependence, because it summarizes only average linear co-movement. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [correlation page](correlation.qmd) standardizes covariance to remove its units.
